claims.text: Equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi has low hardness and strength in a simple solid-solution state because its microstructure offers few intrinsic obstacles to dislocation motion.
A controlled thermomechanical treatment can induce fine precipitates or enhanced dislocation networks in CoCrFeNiTi.
Fine precipitates or enhanced dislocation networks will introduce additional barriers to dislocation glide.
Introducing nanoscale barriers will increase the hardness and yield strength of CoCrFeNiTi.
The initial CoCrFeNiTi state is a homogeneous single-phase solid solution with moderate lattice distortion.
The secondary thermomechanical treatment is intended to change the obstacle population without changing overall alloy composition.
The controlled comparison uses room-temperature, quasi-static nanoindentation and uniaxial mechanical testing.
Treated and untreated samples should have the same prior processing history apart from the secondary treatment.
The relevant structural mediator is the density and spatial distribution of nanoscale precipitates or dislocation arrangements.
Limited lattice distortion and chemical homogeneity provide minimal resistance to dislocation motion in simple-solid-solution CoCrFeNiTi.
Low resistance to dislocation motion produces high plasticity together with low hardness and strength.
Nanoscale obstacles increase the critical resolved shear stress required for plastic flow.
Treated specimens should show statistically significant increases in both hardness and yield strength relative to untreated specimens.
TEM or SEM should reveal additional nanoscale features that act as barriers to dislocation propagation in treated specimens.
The as-cast or as-annealed baseline is a homogeneous, single-phase CoCrFeNiTi solid solution.
The baseline has high ductility but relatively low hardness and yield strength because dislocation glide is unobstructed.
The hypothesis is restricted to equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi under ambient, quasi-static loading.
The fundamentals of solid-solution hardening and plastic deformation in equiatomic high-entropy alloys remain incompletely characterized.
The relative contributions of dynamic recovery and the absence of robust intrinsic barriers remain unquantified in CoCrFeNiTi.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant hardness and yield-strength increase, or failure to detect additional nanoscale obstacles, would falsify the proposed explanation.

contradictions.description: The intervention permits formation of fine precipitates, which are secondary phases, while the boundary says the alloy is maintained in a single-phase solid-solution state. The exception for 'controlled nanoscale obstacle formation' softens but does not resolve this structural-state inconsistency.

The rule treats failure to detect newly created obstacles as falsification, but that result could simply mean the unspecified treatment failed to implement the intended mediator rather than disproving the proposed obstacle-strengthening mechanism.
